opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the starting point for me is dissatisfaction with the two dominant framings. One is "align AI to human preferences," which runs into the problem that preferences are messy, inconsistent, sometimes ill-informed, and, more fundamentally, they don't settle whose preferences count when people disagree. The other is "align AI to some universal set of human values," which sounds nice but tends to smuggle in a single moral theory that lots of reasonable people would reject.

Social roles offer something in between that I think is much more workable. If you look at how humans actually manage to cooperate with each other despite deep disagreement about values, a lot of it runs through roles. We have pretty rich, shared understandings of what it means to be a good doctor, a good lawyer, a good teacher, a good contractor, or a good assistant. Those norms aren't arbitrary, and they aren't just "do whatever your principal wants." A good doctor respects patient autonomy but won't prescribe something harmful just because you asked. A good lawyer advocates zealously for a client but won't help them commit fraud. The role carries obligations to the person being served and to third parties and society.

So rather than asking "what does this user want?" or "what is the one true good?", the question becomes: what role is this AI system playing, and what are the norms that people in a society would reasonably agree should govern that role? That's a more tractable question. It's grounded in existing practices we can study, it's pluralistic, since different roles have different norms and different communities can negotiate them, and it naturally builds in limits on helpfulness that aren't ad hoc.

It also gives us a better account of legitimacy. Role norms are something like social contracts. They emerge from, and can be revised by, the stakeholders affected. That points toward alignment as an ongoing, democratic process of norm-setting rather than an engineering problem with a fixed target someone gets to define in private.

Finally, it's helpful technically. An AI that understands itself as occupying a role has to model not just what you literally said, but the context, the expectations attached to the relationship, and when deference is appropriate versus when it should push back. That is the kind of contextual, norm-sensitive reasoning I think we actually want, and it's something we can try to formalize and learn from human behavior, rather than hoping it falls out of preference maximization.

r001.rationale: The response explains that AI systems can be understood through their roles, but it does not state that increasingly agentic systems can still be understood this way.

r002.rationale: It frames alignment around the norms governing the role an AI system plays and describes role-sensitive, norm-guided behavior as the target.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short version is that I think the dominant framings of alignment, the ones that talk about aligning AI with "human values" or "human preferences" in the abstract, are trying to answer a question that doesn't actually have a well-defined answer. There is no single set of human values. People disagree, deeply and reasonably, and even individual people have preferences that are inconsistent, context-dependent, and change over time. So when you say "align the AI with human values," you've smuggled in an assumption that there's some aggregate object out there to aim at, and I just don't think there is.

Roles give you a different starting point. If you look at how we actually hold humans to standards of good behavior, we almost never ask "is this person aligned with humanity's values?" We ask whether they're a good doctor, a good teacher, a good contractor, a good friend. Each of those roles comes with a set of norms and obligations that are fairly well-specified, that have been worked out over long stretches of social practice, and crucially that are legible to the other people in the relationship. A doctor has duties of care, confidentiality, informed consent. Those aren't derived from some universal utility function. They're the accumulated institutional answer to the question "what do we need from someone occupying this position?"

And I think that's exactly the right question to ask about AI systems. We're not building a single oracle that has to represent all of humanity. We're building systems that get deployed as assistants, as tutors, as research aids, as customer service agents, as tools inside organizations. Each of those deployments is a role, and each role already has, or could be given, a reasonably clear specification of what it means to do it well and what it means to overstep. That makes the alignment target something you can actually evaluate, contest, and revise, rather than something you have to guess at by inferring hidden preferences.

There's also a normative reason I like it, not just a practical one. Role-based norms tend to encode constraints on power. A good employee doesn't just maximize the boss's stated goals. They refuse unethical instructions, they don't go beyond their remit, they defer to others on things outside their competence. Those constraints exist precisely because we've learned that people in roles can do a lot of damage if they treat their role as license to pursue some objective by any means. A lot of what worries me about AI, the scenarios where a system takes drastic unilateral action because it inferred that's what the user "really wanted," are failures that a role-based framing rules out by construction. An assistant that understands its role knows that acting outside it isn't being more helpful, it's being a worse assistant.

So I'd put it this way: roles let you replace the question "what does this AI value?" with "what is this AI for, and what does doing that well require, including what it should not do?" I think that second question is one we actually know how to make progress on, because it's the one human societies have been answering for a very long time.

r001.rationale: The response frames deployed AI systems as assistants, tutors, research aids, and other roles, but it does not state that increasingly agentic systems can still be understood that way.

r002.rationale: It identifies alignment with what a system is for and what doing that role well requires—including limits on its behavior—as the target.

astra-6.text:
I think social roles are useful because they make the alignment question more concrete. Instead of asking, “How do we align an AI with human values?” in the abstract, we can ask, “What does it mean for this system to be a good teacher, a good assistant, or a good collaborator?” Those roles come with expectations about what you should do, whose interests you should take into account, and what limits there are on your authority.

A teacher, for example, shouldn’t just give a student whatever answer they want. Sometimes being a good teacher means challenging them or helping them work through a problem themselves. And being someone’s assistant doesn’t mean you should follow every instruction regardless of how it affects other people. So alignment can’t simply mean satisfying the immediate preferences of whoever is interacting with the system.

The useful thing about roles is that they situate those obligations within a relationship and a broader social context. They also give us a vocabulary for disagreement: Is the system overstepping? Is it neglecting a responsibility? Should it defer to someone else? That doesn’t resolve every question, because roles themselves can be contested or unjust. But it gives us a more grounded starting point for deciding what we want AI systems to do, and for holding them accountable.

r001.rationale: The response explains how roles such as teacher, assistant, and collaborator make alignment concrete, but does not mention increasingly agentic AI systems.

r002.rationale: It frames alignment around what it means for a system to be a good teacher, assistant, or collaborator, presenting good performance of its role as the alignment aim.

sol-6.1.text:
I think social roles give us a way to make alignment more concrete. When we ask whether an AI is aligned, the immediate question is: aligned with whom, and in what capacity? We don’t expect the same behavior from a teacher, a doctor, a friend, or an employee. Each role comes with different responsibilities, different permissions, and different limits on whose wishes should be followed.

A doctor, for example, shouldn’t simply do whatever a patient requests. They have responsibilities to the patient’s health, to informed consent, and to professional standards. Similarly, an AI assistant shouldn’t necessarily satisfy every immediate preference its user expresses. What it should do depends on the relationship it’s supposed to have with that user, and its obligations to other people affected by its actions.

So I see social roles as a useful intermediate level between very abstract values, like human well-being, and very specific instructions. They help us ask: What is this system entrusted to do? Who can hold it accountable? When should it defer, and when should it push back? Those are questions we need to answer to give alignment a practical target.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI’s intended social roles, but does not state that increasingly agentic systems can still be understood through those roles.

r002.rationale: It presents social roles as a practical alignment target and explains that the AI’s responsibilities and behavior should depend on the role it is entrusted to fulfill.
